lessons.concept: Start with a question a shop actually needs answered: two products cost 349 MAD each and receive a ten percent discount; what amount should the page display? explanation.title: From a shop question to values
explanation.text: A name is a label attached to a value. const prevents moving that label to another value; it does not lock every drawer inside a labeled object.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: A declaration introduces a name in a scope. In let quantity = 2, let declares the binding, quantity names it and the equals sign initializes it with the number 2. Later, quantity = quantity + 1 reads the current value, computes 3 and assigns that result back to the binding. It is not an algebraic equality. A const declaration also creates a binding, but subsequent assignment to that binding is forbidden. Prefer const for inputs that do not change during a calculation, and let for a value whose reassignment is intentional. Neither keyword makes a value globally available everywhere; the containing block or function determines where the name can be used.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: The type belongs to a value. The number 2 and the string '2' are different values even though they look similar when printed. A string represents text; a number supports arithmetic; a boolean represents true or false. undefined often means a value has not been provided, whereas null is commonly used as an explicit absence marker. JavaScript also has bigint and symbol primitives, but this lab uses ordinary numbers. Objects collect named properties, and arrays collect ordered elements. typeof is useful evidence, not a complete validator: typeof NaN is 'number', and typeof null is 'object' for historical reasons. We therefore check the particular property our calculation needs, rather than accepting every value whose type name sounds appropriate.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: Trace expressions before trusting their output. With a price of 349 and quantity 2, multiplication produces 698; multiplying by 0.1 produces a discount of 69.8; subtraction produces the intended total of 628.2. Multiplication normally takes precedence over addition. Parentheses make a different evaluation order explicit, so (10 + 5) * 2 is 30 while 10 + 5 * 2 is 20. The plus operator is particularly dangerous at a text boundary: '349' + 2 produces the text '3492'. Subtraction and multiplication have different conversion behavior, so a successful multiplication is not evidence that incoming data already has the correct type. Normalize inputs explicitly and keep units in variable names.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: A form field normally gives your program text, even when the user types digits. Number('2') produces the number 2, but Number('') and Number('   ') produce zero. Number('2e2') accepts exponent notation and Number('0x10') accepts hexadecimal notation. Those conversions are valid language behavior; they are not necessarily valid shop quantities. Decide the accepted text format before conversion. Our rule accepts a trimmed sequence of decimal digits, then requires an integer from 1 through 99. It accepts surrounding spaces and leading zeros deliberately. It rejects a decimal point, a sign, exponent notation, a blank value and any trailing letters. A different product may choose another contract, but that contract must be stated and tested.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: The complete solution introduces functions to avoid repeating the same validation. A function declaration gives a sequence of statements a name and names its incoming parameters. Calling parseQuantity('2') runs that sequence with raw bound to the string '2'. return gives a value back to the caller. if runs its block only when its condition is true; throw creates an error and stops the current path unless a caller catches it. In the guard, || means that either defect is enough to reject the input. Its short-circuit behavior matters: when raw is not a string, JavaScript does not evaluate raw.trim(). This prevents an unrelated method error from hiding the intentional validation message.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: Read /^[0-9]+$/ as a small format rule, not magic punctuation to memorize. The slashes delimit a regular expression. The caret anchors the beginning, [0-9] permits a decimal digit, the plus sign requires one or more digits, and the dollar sign anchors the end. The test method reports whether the trimmed input matches the whole pattern. The exclamation mark negates that result. trim removes surrounding whitespace and returns a new string; it does not edit the original string. After the format check, Number performs conversion, and Number.isSafeInteger rejects fractions, infinities, NaN and integers outside the reliably represented range. The later bounds check adds the shop-specific maximum of 99.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: Ordinary JavaScript numbers use binary floating-point representation. Some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Display formatting can hide that difference without changing the stored number. For this teaching model, store money as integer centimes: 349 MAD becomes 34900 centimes. Store a percentage in basis points, where 10000 means one hundred percent and 1000 means ten percent. Multiplication then uses integer operands. This is a useful design for a currency with two decimal places, not a universal money library. Taxes, multiple currencies, refunds and legal rounding rules need separately specified policies. We define one nonnegative discount rounded to the nearest centime for this single line item.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: Integer storage still has a limit. Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991; beyond it, neighboring mathematical integers may map to the same JavaScript number. Validate intermediate results as well as inputs. A safe unit price multiplied by a safe quantity can produce an unsafe subtotal; a safe subtotal multiplied by 1000 can produce an unsafe discount numerator. The solution rejects either case before using the result. This intentionally rejects some enormous amounts even when the final discounted amount would be small. That conservative contract is easier to explain and test than silently accepting lost precision. A larger-range implementation would require a separate BigInt or decimal design, including an explicit rounding algorithm and serialization rules.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: calculateCart accepts already normalized numeric inputs. Number.isSafeInteger does not coerce a string into a number, so passing '2' directly is rejected even though parseQuantity('2') succeeds. The price may be zero, quantity must be positive and no larger than 99, and discountBps must be between zero and 10000 inclusive. First compute subtotalCents, then discountNumerator, then validate both. Math.round chooses the nearest integer centime; with our nonnegative values an exact half rounds upward. Finally subtract discountCents from subtotalCents. For 34900, 2 and 1000 the intermediate values are 69800, 69800000, 6980 and 62820. Writing this trace makes it clear where a mistaken division by 100 instead of 10000 would first diverge.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: The return statement builds an object containing three named results. In { subtotalCents, discountCents, totalCents }, each short property name means the same thing as subtotalCents: subtotalCents for that property. The function creates a fresh result instead of editing an existing cart. Property access such as cart.totalCents reads one named value. The final log uses ...cart to copy those properties into a display object, then adds label. This spread makes a shallow copy; nested objects would still be shared. Our result contains only primitive numbers, so that nested-reference issue does not arise here. Do not generalize this small example into a claim that spread deeply clones every shopping-cart structure.

explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: const protects a binding, not every object reachable through it. If const item = { stock: 3 }, item.stock = 2 is allowed because the binding still points to the same object. Assigning a different object to item would fail. If alias = item, both names identify that same object, so a change through alias is visible through item. By contrast, a copied primitive number does not track later reassignments to another variable. explanation.title: Understand each boundary
explanation.text: Formatting belongs at the display boundary. (628.2).toFixed(2) returns the string '628.20', not a more precise number. Adding 1 to that string concatenates, whereas adding 1 to the original number performs arithmetic. A template literal uses backticks and evaluates each expression inside a dollar-sign brace pair, then inserts its textual representation. Our formatter keeps integer centimes until it creates the label: Math.floor divides out whole dirhams, the remainder operator finds the remaining centimes, String converts that remainder to text and padStart adds a leading zero when needed. teaching.what: Start with a question a shop actually needs answered: two products cost 349 MAD each and receive a ten percent discount; what amount should the page display? A computer does not understand the sentence until we represent its quantities and operations. The input is a unit price, a quantity and a discount rate. The transformation multiplies price by quantity, calculates a discount and subtracts it. The output is a new amount, then a readable label. These stages are deliberately separate: a label containing MAD is useful to a person, but it is unsuitable as the input of a multiplication. This lesson develops that separation before building a reusable calculator.
teaching.why: Use a plain JavaScript file and Node, with no browser, network, packages or database. From the repository root, run node academy-labs/06-javascript/values.js. If recreating the lab elsewhere, create the folders first and save the complete solution at that relative path. A terminal command starts Node, which reads the file and executes its statements in order. console.log sends evidence to the terminal; it does not change a web page. Read the first error before changing anything. A missing-file error concerns your working directory or filename, whereas a SyntaxError concerns the program text. Run each smaller example separately so that identical variable names do not collide in one file.

teaching.how:
A declaration introduces a name in a scope. In let quantity = 2, let declares the binding, quantity names it and the equals sign initializes it with the number 2. Later, quantity = quantity + 1 reads the current value, computes 3 and assigns that result back to the binding. It is not an algebraic equality. A const declaration also creates a binding, but subsequent assignment to that binding is forbidden. Prefer const for inputs that do not change during a calculation, and let for a value whose reassignment is intentional. Neither keyword makes a value globally available everywhere; the containing block or function determines where the name can be used.
The type belongs to a value. The number 2 and the string '2' are different values even though they look similar when printed. A string represents text; a number supports arithmetic; a boolean represents true or false. undefined often means a value has not been provided, whereas null is commonly used as an explicit absence marker. JavaScript also has bigint and symbol primitives, but this lab uses ordinary numbers. Objects collect named properties, and arrays collect ordered elements. typeof is useful evidence, not a complete validator: typeof NaN is 'number', and typeof null is 'object' for historical reasons. We therefore check the particular property our calculation needs, rather than accepting every value whose type name sounds appropriate.
Trace expressions before trusting their output. With a price of 349 and quantity 2, multiplication produces 698; multiplying by 0.1 produces a discount of 69.8; subtraction produces the intended total of 628.2. Multiplication normally takes precedence over addition. Parentheses make a different evaluation order explicit, so (10 + 5) * 2 is 30 while 10 + 5 * 2 is 20. The plus operator is particularly dangerous at a text boundary: '349' + 2 produces the text '3492'. Subtraction and multiplication have different conversion behavior, so a successful multiplication is not evidence that incoming data already has the correct type. Normalize inputs explicitly and keep units in variable names.
A form field normally gives your program text, even when the user types digits. Number('2') produces the number 2, but Number('') and Number('   ') produce zero. Number('2e2') accepts exponent notation and Number('0x10') accepts hexadecimal notation. Those conversions are valid language behavior; they are not necessarily valid shop quantities. Decide the accepted text format before conversion. Our rule accepts a trimmed sequence of decimal digits, then requires an integer from 1 through 99. It accepts surrounding spaces and leading zeros deliberately. It rejects a decimal point, a sign, exponent notation, a blank value and any trailing letters. A different product may choose another contract, but that contract must be stated and tested.
The complete solution introduces functions to avoid repeating the same validation. A function declaration gives a sequence of statements a name and names its incoming parameters. Calling parseQuantity('2') runs that sequence with raw bound to the string '2'. return gives a value back to the caller. if runs its block only when its condition is true; throw creates an error and stops the current path unless a caller catches it. In the guard, || means that either defect is enough to reject the input. Its short-circuit behavior matters: when raw is not a string, JavaScript does not evaluate raw.trim(). This prevents an unrelated method error from hiding the intentional validation message.
Read /^[0-9]+$/ as a small format rule, not magic punctuation to memorize. The slashes delimit a regular expression. The caret anchors the beginning, [0-9] permits a decimal digit, the plus sign requires one or more digits, and the dollar sign anchors the end. The test method reports whether the trimmed input matches the whole pattern. The exclamation mark negates that result. trim removes surrounding whitespace and returns a new string; it does not edit the original string. After the format check, Number performs conversion, and Number.isSafeInteger rejects fractions, infinities, NaN and integers outside the reliably represented range. The later bounds check adds the shop-specific maximum of 99.
Ordinary JavaScript numbers use binary floating-point representation. Some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Display formatting can hide that difference without changing the stored number. For this teaching model, store money as integer centimes: 349 MAD becomes 34900 centimes. Store a percentage in basis points, where 10000 means one hundred percent and 1000 means ten percent. Multiplication then uses integer operands. This is a useful design for a currency with two decimal places, not a universal money library. Taxes, multiple currencies, refunds and legal rounding rules need separately specified policies. We define one nonnegative discount rounded to the nearest centime for this single line item.
Integer storage still has a limit. Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991; beyond it, neighboring mathematical integers may map to the same JavaScript number. Validate intermediate results as well as inputs. A safe unit price multiplied by a safe quantity can produce an unsafe subtotal; a safe subtotal multiplied by 1000 can produce an unsafe discount numerator. The solution rejects either case before using the result. This intentionally rejects some enormous amounts even when the final discounted amount would be small. That conservative contract is easier to explain and test than silently accepting lost precision. A larger-range implementation would require a separate BigInt or decimal design, including an explicit rounding algorithm and serialization rules.
calculateCart accepts already normalized numeric inputs. Number.isSafeInteger does not coerce a string into a number, so passing '2' directly is rejected even though parseQuantity('2') succeeds. The price may be zero, quantity must be positive and no larger than 99, and discountBps must be between zero and 10000 inclusive. First compute subtotalCents, then discountNumerator, then validate both. Math.round chooses the nearest integer centime; with our nonnegative values an exact half rounds upward. Finally subtract discountCents from subtotalCents. For 34900, 2 and 1000 the intermediate values are 69800, 69800000, 6980 and 62820. Writing this trace makes it clear where a mistaken division by 100 instead of 10000 would first diverge.
The return statement builds an object containing three named results. In { subtotalCents, discountCents, totalCents }, each short property name means the same thing as subtotalCents: subtotalCents for that property. The function creates a fresh result instead of editing an existing cart. Property access such as cart.totalCents reads one named value. The final log uses ...cart to copy those properties into a display object, then adds label. This spread makes a shallow copy; nested objects would still be shared. Our result contains only primitive numbers, so that nested-reference issue does not arise here. Do not generalize this small example into a claim that spread deeply clones every shopping-cart structure.
const protects a binding, not every object reachable through it. If const item = { stock: 3 }, item.stock = 2 is allowed because the binding still points to the same object. Assigning a different object to item would fail. If alias = item, both names identify that same object, so a change through alias is visible through item. By contrast, a copied primitive number does not track later reassignments to another variable. The reference example adds a nested details object to demonstrate why { ...item } is not enough to isolate nested changes. Before modifying a real cart, identify which objects are shared and which properties need copying; otherwise an apparently local edit can unexpectedly change another screen's state.
Formatting belongs at the display boundary. (628.2).toFixed(2) returns the string '628.20', not a more precise number. Adding 1 to that string concatenates, whereas adding 1 to the original number performs arithmetic. A template literal uses backticks and evaluates each expression inside a dollar-sign brace pair, then inserts its textual representation. Our formatter keeps integer centimes until it creates the label: Math.floor divides out whole dirhams, the remainder operator finds the remaining centimes, String converts that remainder to text and padStart adds a leading zero when needed. A five-centime amount therefore displays as 0.05 MAD. The formatter validates its input instead of disguising invalid money as a plausible label.
Build the exercise in stages and verify each boundary. First reproduce the declarations and conversion examples and explain their logs without running them. Next implement parseQuantity and test '2', ' 02 ', '', '2.5', '2e2', '2x', '0' and '100'. Then implement the numeric calculator and compare every returned property, not just the final label. Try no discount, a full discount, a zero price and a one-centime price with a half discount. Finally freeze an input object, pass its numeric properties to the calculator and confirm they remain unchanged. An error should stop an invalid calculation rather than manufacture a zero total. Test the complete lab from the repository root with node --test lecomax-learning-app/tests/javascript-values.test.cjs.
Debug in the order data crosses boundaries. If you see '3492', log each operand and its typeof before changing the formula; that is useful diagnosis, not yet a correction. Apply the correction where text enters the program, then rerun valid and invalid cases. If NaN appears, find the first conversion that produced it; comparing a value with NaN using === cannot detect it, whereas Number.isNaN can. If a const assignment fails, decide whether reassignment is actually needed instead of changing every declaration to let. This calculator is an isolated exercise, not the site's payment implementation. A real checkout must obtain authoritative prices, discounts and stock on the server and define rounding across all line items before accepting payment.

lessons.concept: Execution flow chooses paths from Boolean expressions and repeats a block over a collection. An error is a structured outcome signaling a contract cannot be honored. The stack trace links failure to preceding calls; modules make contracts explicit through imports and exports. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

throw interrupts normal flow; catch should recover meaningfully or enrich and rethrow. The first stack frame belonging to the project is often the best diagnostic start. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

Validate arguments at entry, choose precise TypeError or RangeError, avoid silent catches, and export small testable functions without global effects. Finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. Short changes make cause and effect easy to connect.
